title: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
claim: Our structured model stays accurate when test-time inputs leave the training range, while baselines degrade sharply.
layout: 2 panels: left stacked time-series samples, right three bar charts; ablations shaded
description: Panel (a), on the left, shows two stacked time-series examples. The EPF DE sample is on top and the Favorita sample is below. In each, an upper green curve is the exogenous input. A dashed line marks the maximum training value, and a grey band marks the region where the input exceeds it. A lower plot shows the target variable. The ground truth is a black line, SLiDE is a dashed orange-red line, and baselines such as TimeXer, GCGNet and TSMixer are dashed in other colors. SLiDE tracks the ground truth more closely in the grey band. Panel (b), on the right, has three grouped bar charts: EPF DE with MSE, Favorita with RMSLE, and Bouc-Wen with MAE. Each chart compares out-of-range and in-range bars for SLiDE (orange) and the baselines (blue). A grey 'Ablations' region sits at the right end of each chart. The eye goes first to the orange bars, which are lower than the blue ones.
caption: SLiDE generalizes well to shifted exogenous inputs, including out-of-range (OOR) input values and unseen test-time input processes. Left: top, an EPF-DE sample in which the wind forecast exceeds the maximum training value, and bottom, a Favorita sample in which the number of related promoted items (log-scale) exceeds the training range. In both cases, SLiDE stays closer to the ground truth than the baselines. Right: SLiDE reduces MSE by 20% on OOR EPF-DE samples and MAE by 30% on the Bouc-Wen transfer task, where models are tested on an unseen forcing process. Ablations show that the structured encoder and linear rollout are critical for shifted-input performance, as shown by an 18% lower RMSLE relative to ablations on OOR Favorita samples.
abstract: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.
